content: To reduce the number of leprosy cases detected among contacts, programs have two options: either treat 100 leprosy contacts without providing chemoprophylaxis or administer chemoprophylaxis to all contacts while treating only 43 leprosy patients. The latter approach is often the preferred choice for many programs. This document provides detailed guidance on implementing contact screening and chemoprophylaxis using single-dose rifampicin. The outlined steps include counseling and obtaining consent, identifying and listing index cases, listing and tracing contacts, screening contacts, and administering prophylactic drugs. Managerial aspects such as planning, training, supervision, and drug management are also addressed. Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, has been recognized since ancient times. The introduction of multidrug therapy (MDT) in the 1980s brought significant hope, leading to the global elimination of leprosy as a public health problem by 2000 and in most countries by 2005. However, over the past decade, the annual global detection of new cases has remained above 200,000. In some countries, active case-finding efforts have revealed hidden cases within communities. Contact tracing has proven to be an effective method for detecting these cases, as contacts of leprosy patients are at a significantly higher risk of infection compared to the general population. Despite the success of MDT in curing leprosy, passive case detection and treatment alone have not been sufficient to interrupt transmission. Various prophylactic regimens, including dapsone, acedapsone, rifampicin, ofloxacin, and minocycline (ROM), have been tested, but the evidence was insufficient to incorporate them into routine programs. A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that single-dose rifampicin (SDR) reduced the incidence of new leprosy cases among contacts by 57%. Subsequent studies in countries such as Morocco, India, Indonesia, Nepal, and Tanzania have shown that SDR chemoprophylaxis can be effectively implemented as part of routine leprosy control activities, significantly reducing the number of new cases. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with SDR for all contacts of leprosy patients. This approach, combined with contact screening, is a major public health intervention. Screening helps identify hidden cases, while PEP reduces the risk of future leprosy among healthy contacts. Household contacts are the most accessible group for detection, but achieving wide coverage of all contact types maximizes the population-level impact. Involving family members, affected individuals, and community leaders is crucial for the success of these interventions. Counseling plays a critical role in obtaining informed consent from index patients to disclose their disease status to household, neighbor, or social contacts. It also motivates healthy contacts to participate in screening and chemoprophylaxis. This technical guide provides practical instructions for implementing contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis under routine program conditions. It is intended for use by national and sub-national program managers, healthcare providers, partners, and community members. The glossary defines key terms used in the document. For example, chemoprophylaxis refers to the prevention of infectious diseases using chemical agents or drugs, such as rifampicin, to prevent leprosy in individuals exposed to a leprosy patient. An index case is a person diagnosed with leprosy for the first time, while a source case refers to an untreated patient who may have transmitted the infection to others. Contacts are individuals who have had prolonged close proximity to a leprosy patient, such as family members, neighbors, or coworkers. Household contacts live in the same dwelling as the index case, while neighbor contacts live nearby, typically within 100 meters. Social contacts include individuals with prolonged contact in settings such as schools or workplaces. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment remain the cornerstone of leprosy control, aiming to halt the transmission of Mycobacterium leprae and prevent disability.
